learning_outcomes.text: Systematic knowledge of the key aspects of mechanical design in industrial engineering and the related methodologies, including the ability to identify the most appropriate methods for defining a product and its characteristics. Knowledge and understanding encompass materials technology, the mechanical design of components and assemblies, their sizing, the study of their static and dynamic behaviour and component interactions, manufacturing technologies, and their graphical representation.
Knowledge of industrial electrical engineering, electrical machines, industrial robotics, and control systems employed in industrial plants.
Knowledge of current topics concerning the organization and management of the technical aspects of production.
Knowledge of information technologies and their role in supporting engineering design. Understanding of data organization within databases and of information systems supporting engineering processes.

Ability to select and apply appropriate analytical, modelling, and experimental methods for the design, analysis, and testing of fluid machinery, thermal engines, and energy conversion systems, including: the application of design principles for thermal and fluid systems; the application of thermodynamic principles to engineering systems; the understanding of major thermodynamic cycles and diagrams; the identification of heat transfer mechanisms relevant to engineering applications; the functional design of turbomachinery, energy conversion plants, and internal combustion engines; and the evaluation of the energy, economic, and environmental performance of fluid machinery, thermal systems, and hydraulic components.

Ability to identify, formulate, and solve industrial engineering problems, particularly in mechanical engineering, by defining technical, social, health, safety, environmental, and commercial constraints and applying established engineering methods to develop engineering projects involving products, devices, machines, energy systems, and automated systems.

Ability to integrate theoretical knowledge and practical skills to solve multidisciplinary engineering problems while considering technical and non-technical constraints and collaborating effectively with engineers and other professionals typically involved in manufacturing industries.
Ability to analyse data and information using established methods and tools, interpret results, and draw consistent conclusions, also with the support of provided guidance.
Ability to compare alternative engineering solutions and contribute to technically justified decisions by referring to engineering standards and established industrial procedures.
Ability to work collaboratively and effectively within a team, understanding the engineering context of a problem and recognizing the main interdisciplinary implications of the application domain.

Ability to organize one's work while meeting assigned deadlines, managing available time and resources effectively, realistically assessing one's own capabilities, and contributing to task prioritization.
Ability to recognize personal knowledge limitations and the need to acquire new competencies by identifying appropriate information sources and guided learning opportunities.

Ability to communicate and convey information, ideas, problems, and solutions in engineering contexts to both specialist and non-specialist audiences, using appropriate technical language and referring to familiar application scenarios.
Ability to present engineering problems, solutions, analyses, and results clearly and systematically through written reports and oral presentations, following standard formats and conventions.

Ability to graphically represent and communicate technical data, results, and engineering solutions through the preparation of drawings, diagrams, graphs, and tables, using established tools and conventions.
Ability to acquire and update knowledge in the relevant engineering field, independently, although primarily under guidance, by using established educational resources and learning tools.

Ability to identify and consult bibliographic sources and technical documentation through the main available resources (libraries, databases, technical manuals, and digital resources), selecting relevant information with appropriate guidance.

Ability to learn through project-based and Problem-Based Learning (PBL) methodologies by applying acquired knowledge and engineering tools to case studies and real-world engineering problems of appropriate complexity.

Ability to understand and interpret the fundamental principles of design, manufacturing, and maintenance processes while operating in compliance with quality, safety, and reliability requirements and with reference to the main international technical and environmental standards (ISO, UNI, ASME, DIN, etc.).

syllabus_topics: Presentation of the course; explanation about examinations
Basic definitions: machine, kinematic chain, mechanism
Kinematic pairs, elementary kinematic pairs (rotational, helical, prismatic) and higher kinematic pairs in the plane and in three-dimensional space

Computation of the degrees of freedom (DOFs) of a plane mechanism (Grübler rule) and a spatial mechanism (Kutzbach rule); Bi-dimensional examples: four-bar linkage, crank, cam follower, cam follower with roller, cross connector, cross connector with ineffective auction; spatial examples: spatial four-bar mechanism with 4 revolute pairs, spatial four-bar mechanism with two revolute, a spherical and a cylindrical joint.
Sliding friction: Coulomb's law, friction coefficient and friction angle
Definition of boundary lubrication, hydrostatic lubrication (natural and forced) and hydrodynamic lubrication (hard and soft)
Rolling friction: definition of the rolling friction parameter and rolling friction coefficient. Friction between dry surfaces, Reye's hypothesis: push pin, flat sled.
Reye hypothesis: brake blocks (only evolution of the pressures on the contact surface, assuming a given direction of approach)
Definition of mechanical efficiency and loss factor
Efficiency of machines in series and in parallel with examples. Efficiency in forward and reverse motion with definition of non back-driveability .
Theoretical Treatment of static problems and kinetostatic
Cardinal equations of statics as a result of the dynamic equations
Rigid body subjected to two forces, two forces and a moment, three forces, three forces and a moment, four forces- Examples: four-bar mechanism and crank thrust (only ideal case).
Mechanical efficiency of the inclined plane; forces exchanged in a rotational joint in the ideal case, and with friction
Definition of the friction circle
Efficiency of the rotational joint
Efficiency of the prismatic joint
Efficiency of the screw-nut pair.
Efficiency of the screw-nut torque, direct and reverse motion
Relationships between the characteristic angles of the thread
The wheel in locomotion: driven wheel, traction and braking
Example of vehicle moving on a horizontal road.
Kinetostatics exercise: crankshaft with friction
Recall kinematic circular rigid motions, rolling curve (roulette) and fixed curve in plane motions
Kinematic analysis of four-bar mechanisms, analytical formulation for crankshaft
Cams and tappets
Kinetostatics exercise: ideal case, case with friction.
Gearing, introduction to mating profiles
Geometry of gears with involute teeth profile

Definition of conjugate profiles and methods for their generation; definition of involute and evolute curves; spur gears with involute teeth: basic properties; geometric characteristics and design: pitch, normal pitch (module), etc.; conditions of continuity of the motion and of non-interference; hints on cutting gears; correction of the toothed wheels and mounting of the same; notes on the spur gears with helical teeth.
Ordinary and planetary gear trains with 1 DOF
Two-DOFs gearing: automotive differential
Mechanical systems with flexible organs: transmissions with belts
Ordinary and pulley blocks, belt brakes
Introduction to the theory of lubrication, deduction of Reynolds’ equation starting from Navier-Stokes’ ones; application to the case of the flat slide: Reynolds’ equation
Application to the case of the flat sled: infinitely wide sled, finite width slide, infinitely narrow sled. Reynolds equation
Infinitely long rotational joint, finite length rotational joint, infinitely short rotational joint, Reynolds’ equation and examples
Lubrication for juxtaposition, Reynolds’ equation and examples
Thrust bearing, journal bearing
Recalls of Newtonian dynamics. Recalls of Lagrangian dynamics: non-redundant formulation
Lagrangian dynamics recalls: redundant formulation and examples
Kinematics and dynamics of crankshaft mechanism: equation of motion
Dynamic balancing of single-cylinder engines
Dynamic balancing multi-cylinder engines

assessment_methods.method: Oral exam with 3 or 4 questions on theoretical and practical issues, with at least one exercise.

assessment_rules: The final grade is based on an oral exam with 3 or 4 questions, including at least one exercise. Grading criteria range from 'Fail' for serious conceptual errors to 'Excellent or outstanding' for complete, in-depth knowledge and critical thinking, with honors awarded for brilliance and originality. Scores range from 18-22 for sufficient understanding, to 29-30 for excellent, and honors beyond that.
